## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
1 + 1
```

You can add options to executable code like this

```{r}
#| echo: false
2 * 2
```

The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed).

```{r}
# R Script to Read and Plot a Shapefile using sf and ggplot2

# 1. Load Required Libraries
# 'sf' is the modern standard for handling spatial vector data (shapefiles, etc.)
# 'ggplot2' is used for the visualization
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
# You may need to install these packages if you haven't already:
# install.packages(c("sf", "ggplot2"))


# 2. Define the Shapefile Path
# IMPORTANT: This assumes 'grt_sites_COMPLETE_100_percent.shp' is in your current R working directory.
# If it's located elsewhere, replace the filename below with the full path,
# e.g., shp_file <- "C:/Users/YourName/Documents/gis_data/grt_sites_COMPLETE_100_percent.shp"
shp_file <- "grt_sites_COMPLETE_100_percent.shp"


# 3. Read the Shapefile
# The st_read function automatically loads all necessary files (.shp, .dbf, .shx, etc.)
# associated with the shapefile.
if (file.exists(shp_file)) {
  cat("Reading shapefile:", shp_file, "\n")
  shp_data <- st_read(shp_file)
  
  # Optional: View the structure and coordinate reference system (CRS)
  # print(head(shp_data))
  # print(st_crs(shp_data))
  
  # 4. Create the ggplot Map
  # geom_sf is a special geometry that understands how to plot simple feature objects
  # and automatically handles coordinate transformations.
  p <- ggplot(data = shp_data) +
    # Your output confirms the Geometry type is POINT. We adjust the aesthetics.
    # We use shape=21 (a filled circle) so 'fill' colors the interior and 'color' colors the border.
    geom_sf(
      shape = 21,              # Use shape 21 (circle that accepts fill and color)
      fill = "darkred",        # Interior color of the points
      color = "white",         # Border color of the points (for contrast)
      size = 3,                # Size of points (3 is a good default)
      alpha = 0.8              # Transparency
    ) +
    # 5. Customize the Plot
    theme_minimal() + # Use a clean, minimal theme
    labs(
      title = "Geographic Plot of GRT Sites (100% Complete)",
      subtitle = paste("Number of Features:", nrow(shp_data)),
      caption = paste("CRS:", st_crs(shp_data)$input),
      x = "Longitude",
      y = "Latitude"
    ) +
    # Ensure aspect ratio is correct for geographic maps
    coord_sf()
  
  # 6. Display the Plot
  print(p)
  
} else {
  # Handle the case where the file is not found
  cat("ERROR: Shapefile not found at the specified path:\n")
  cat(shp_file, "\n")
  cat("Please ensure all shapefile components (.shp, .dbf, .shx, etc.) are in the directory \n")
  cat("or update the 'shp_file' variable with the correct full path.\n")
}

# Further Customization Ideas:
# 1. To map a variable (e.g., column 'VALUE'):
#    geom_sf(aes(fill = VALUE, color = NA)) +
#    scale_fill_viridis_c() # Use a nice color scale
# 2. To add background geometry (like country/state borders) for context, you could use 
#    the 'rnaturalearth' package and add its features with another geom_sf layer.
# 3. Since your data is POINTS, try mapping one of the 13 attributes to color or size:
#    geom_sf(aes(fill = your_column_name, color = your_column_name), shape = 21, size = 3) + 
#    scale_fill_discrete() # or scale_fill_viridis_c() if the column is numeric

```

```{r}
# R Script to Read and Plot a Shapefile using sf and ggplot2

# 1. Load Required Libraries
# Function to check for and install/load packages
load_packages <- function(pkg){
  # Check if package is installed
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    cat(paste0("Package '", pkg, "' not found. Attempting to install...\n"))
    # Install the package
    install.packages(pkg, dependencies = TRUE)
  }
  # Load the package
  library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)
}

# Load 'sf' and 'mapview'
# 'sf' is the modern standard for handling spatial vector data (shapefiles, etc.)
# 'mapview' is used to create interactive Leaflet maps from sf objects
load_packages("sf")
load_packages("mapview")


# 2. Define the Shapefile Path
# IMPORTANT: This assumes 'grt_sites_COMPLETE_100_percent.shp' is in your current R working directory.
# If it's located elsewhere, replace the filename below with the full path,
# e.g., shp_file <- "C:/Users/YourName/Documents/gis_data/grt_sites_COMPLETE_100_percent.shp"
shp_file <- "grt_sites_COMPLETE_100_percent.shp"


# 3. Read the Shapefile
# The st_read function automatically loads all necessary files (.shp, .dbf, .shx, etc.)
# associated with the shapefile.
if (file.exists(shp_file)) {
  cat("Reading shapefile:", shp_file, "\n")
  shp_data <- st_read(shp_file)
  
  # Optional: View the structure and coordinate reference system (CRS)
  # print(head(shp_data))
  # print(st_crs(shp_data))
  
  # 4. Create the INTERACTIVE Map using mapview
  # mapview automatically handles the visualization of POINT geometry
  # and includes zoom, panning, and basemap switching (OpenStreetMap is default).
  # Hovering over a point will display its attributes.
  p <- mapview(
    shp_data, 
    map.title = "Interactive Plot of GRT Sites (100% Complete)",
    layer.name = "GRT Sites",
    col.regions = "darkred", # Color of the points
    cex = 6,                 # Size of the points (slightly larger for visibility)
    alpha = 0.8              # Opacity
  )
  
  # 5. Display the Plot
  # If running in RStudio, this will open the map in the Viewer pane.
  # If running in a script, it will open in your browser.
  print(p)
  
} else {
  # Handle the case where the file is not found
  cat("ERROR: Shapefile not found at the specified path:\n")
  cat(shp_file, "\n")
  cat("Please ensure all shapefile components (.shp, .dbf, .shx, etc.) are in the directory \n")
  cat("or update the 'shp_file' variable with the correct full path.\n")
}

# Further Customization Ideas for Mapview:
# 1. To map a specific variable (e.g., column 'TYPE') to point color:
#    p <- mapview(shp_data, zcol = "TYPE")
# 2. To change the basemap (e.g., use ESRI World Imagery):
#    p <- mapview(shp_data, map.title = "GRT Sites") + mapview(shp = NULL, map.types = "Esri.WorldImagery")
# 3. To display the map without a specific variable:
#    p <- mapview(shp_data, zcol = NULL)

```

```{r}
load_packages("spdep")
# Ensure 'sf' is loaded as well: library(sf)
```

```{r}
# A. Extract Coordinates
# spdep functions often require the coordinates directly, not the sf object.
# We use the st_coordinates() function from the sf package.
coords <- sf::st_coordinates(shp_data)

# B. Define Neighbors using k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
# Define k=4: Each site is connected to its 4 nearest neighbors.
# KNN is good because it ensures every point has a neighbor, even in sparse areas.
k_neighbors <- spdep::knearneigh(coords, k = 4)

# C. Convert Neighbor Structure to a Neighbors List (nb)
# The knearneigh object must be converted to a formal list of neighbors.
nb_list <- spdep::knn2nb(k_neighbors)

# Optional: Visualize the neighbor connections (requires the 'mapview' package)
# mapview::mapview(shp_data) + spdep::spplot.nb(nb_list, coords)
```

```{r}
# Create the weights object (listw) with row standardization
# 'style="W"' performs row standardization: sum(w_ij) = 1 for all i
spatial_weights_w <- spdep::nb2listw(nb_list, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# Optional: View summary of the weights matrix
summary(spatial_weights_w)
```

```{r}
# Check if the column exists and its type
print(names(shp_data))
print(class(shp_data$n))
```

```{r}
# 1. Clean and convert the column to numeric. 
# We use suppressWarnings to handle any NA introduction gracefully.
suppressWarnings({
  shp_data$Residentil <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", shp_data$Residentil))
})

# 2. Check how many values, if any, failed conversion (became NA)
cat("Number of NA values after conversion:", sum(is.na(shp_data$Residentil)), "\n")
```

```{r}
# Assuming shp_data has a numerical column named 'Value'
# Calculate Moran's I statistic
moran_test <- spdep::moran.test(
  shp_data$Residentil, 
  listw = spatial_weights_w,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Print the result
print(moran_test)

# Interpretation: 
# - A positive Moran's I (and a small p-value) indicates **positive spatial autocorrelation** (high values cluster near high values).
# - A negative Moran's I indicates **negative spatial autocorrelation** (high values cluster near low values).
```
